title: The Nanakshahi calendar
hookLine: in 2003 the SGPC adopted a solar Sikh calendar, later revised; Sikhs still discuss which dates to keep

lines: MOON, SUN AND THE WESTERN YEAR.
cards: Is the party on the actual birthday, or the nearest Saturday? Your parents' house, or mine? Which date counts?
Now stretch that question across a whole people spread around the world, with festivals set by the moon, the sun and the Western calendar all at once.
A gurpurab set by the moon can move by weeks from one year to the next. Sikhs have tried to solve that. Today: Nanakshahi.

teach.b: For centuries, Sikh festivals followed the Bikrami calendar, the traditional calendar used across North India. Its months follow the sun, but many holy days are set by the moon, so their dates shift each year.
A Canadian Sikh, Pal Singh Purewal, proposed a new calendar: the Nanakshahi, named for Guru Nanak, its years counted from his birth in 1469.
It uses a solar year that keeps pace with the Western one, so each month begins on the same date every year, and each gurpurab falls on a fixed day. Chet, the first month, begins in mid-March.
In 2003, the SGPC, the body that manages the major gurdwaras in Punjab, adopted it. Its supporters, in Punjab and abroad, welcomed dates you could plan around, a calendar of the community's own.

Others felt something precious was lost: the old link with the moon, and with how their grandparents had kept the days. Even in 2003, a few days, Guru Nanak's gurpurab among them, had stayed with the moon.

In 2010, the SGPC revised the calendar and moved more gurpurabs back to lunar dates. Today the revised calendar is widely followed, and some gurdwaras, in Punjab and abroad, keep the original 2003 version.
Sikhs still discuss it, sometimes with real feeling.
Which dates to keep is a live question, and people of deep faith stand on different sides.
What doesn't change is what the dates are for: to gather, to sing, and to remember the Gurus.

how: Sikh gurdwaras publish yearly calendars of gurpurabs; many follow the SGPC's revised Nanakshahi calendar, and some keep the original 2003 version, so dates can differ between communities.

practice: Think of one Guru you've come to know on this path, and picture how you'd want to remember their day: a shabad, langar, a quiet hour. Let the date matter less than the remembering.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the Guru you chose.
